abstract: Optoretinography (ORG) provides a noninvasive approach for measuring stimulus-evoked photoreceptor responses in the living human retina, but its application to retinal disease using clinically translatable imaging systems remains limited. Here, we applied velocity-based ORG using a clinical-grade swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT) system to assess photoreceptor function in disease-affected human retinas and healthy controls. Following pupil dilation and dark adaptation, repeated B-scans were acquired at 400 Hz during visible-light stimulation using a phase-sensitive 100-kHz, 1060-nm swept-source OCT system. Stimulus-evoked optical path length changes between the inner segment/outer segment junction (IS/OS) and cone outer segment tips (COST) were used to quantify cone outer-segment responses. Healthy retinas exhibited rapid and reproducible responses characterized by an initial outer-segment contraction followed by elongation, whereas disease-affected retinas exhibited quantitatively reduced or altered response amplitudes and temporal dynamics. ORG also detected functional improvement following treatment in a vitamin-A-deficient retina. These findings demonstrate the ability of velocity-based ORG to quantitatively detect photoreceptor dysfunction and functional change using a clinically compatible OCT platform, supporting its potential as a noninvasive functional biomarker for retinal disease and therapeutic response.
